newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh budget aims to fight poverty - minister.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh budget aims to fight poverty - minister.

text.p: Bangladesh Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria on Friday defended his budget proposals for fiscal 1997/98 beginning on July 1, saying they were intended to fight poverty, generate employment and protect local industry.
"We have taken definite and specific steps to ease poverty and ensure social justice," Kibria told a post-budget news conference.

On Thursday, Kibria announced the budget proposing a 81.62-billion-taka ($1.9-billion) deficit for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June). Revenue was seen at 196.24 billion taka against expenditure of 277.86 billion.
He said 23.3 percent of the revenue would be spent on projects that would directly benefit poor people of the country.
Nearly half of Bangladesh's 120 million people live below the poverty line.
Kibria said the government promised adequate funds on subsidies for agriculture, housing and a monthly pension allowance for 450,000 poverty-stricken elderly citizens.
This included setting up a 0.5-billion-taka pension fund, a 0.5-billion-taka housing fund, and providing credit worth up to 10 billion taka for the country's cereal-growers.

"I know it's little. It's a beginning and first step towards ensuring social security," he said. He said the government must pay adequate attention to the development of agriculture as two-thirds of the country's population were dependent on the sector.
Kibria said the budget also envisaged creation of specialised bank for offering credit for self employment.
More than 18 percent of the country's population are unemployed, according to official figure.
The finance minister said he proposed a lower tariff on imported industrial raw materials. "The move aims to protect the domestic industry against competition from imported finished goods," he said.
Commerce and Industry Minister Tofael Ahmed said that local industry was challenged by relatively low-taxed imported goods.
"The drastic trade liberalisation by the previous government had severely hurt our domestic industries," he told the same news conference.
Kibria said the new fiscal measures proposed in the budget would hopefully rationalise the tax rates and encourage domestic industries.

The finance minister rejected criticism by the main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), saying the government, which took office a year ago, would fulfil its pledges to eradicate poverty and establish social justice.
"The budget is not encouraging and faulty. It has not reflected the realities," said BNP central leader and former finance minister Saifur Rahman.
Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's government had failed to manage the economy in the past year and there had been capital flight rather than increases in investment, he said.

Kibria, in his budget speech, forecast more robust growth over the next few years. He predicted annual gross domestic product (GDP) would expand by 7.0 percent between fiscal 1997/98 and 2001/2, against an average 4.5 percent during 1991-96.
The country's economy grew by 5.7 percent in 1996/97 against a target of 5.5 percent. GDP growth was 5.4 percent in 1995/96.
"The economic policies pursued by the government paved the way for this success," Kibria said.

In a bid to boost business activity, Kibria proposed to cut corporate tax for banks, insurance companies and financial institutions to 40 percent from 45 percent. He also proposed reducing the highest rate of customs duty to 42.5 percent for 1997/98 from the present 45 percent.
